questions.question: Consider f(n) = 3n² + 5n log n + 7. Which of the following is TRUE?
options: f(n) = Θ(n²)
f(n) = Θ(n log n)
f(n) = Θ(n³)
f(n) = Θ(n)

solution.concept: Growth of a sum is governed by its fastest-growing term (the dominant term).
steps: The three terms grow as n², n log n and a constant.
n log n = o(n²), because (n log n)/n² = (log n)/n → 0.
So f(n) is squeezed between 3n² and (3+ε)n² for large n.
Hence f(n) = Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Adding a lower-order term such as 5n log n never changes the Θ-class. Students who sum the exponents or pick the largest coefficient by eye get B or C.

questions.question: If f(n) = Θ(g(n)) and g(n) = Θ(h(n)), which statement is necessarily TRUE?
options: f(n) = Θ(h(n))
f(n) = O(h(n)) but f(n) ≠ Θ(h(n))
f(n) = o(h(n))
Nothing can be concluded about f and h

solution.concept: Θ is an equivalence relation: it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
steps: f = Θ(g) gives constants c₁, c₂, n₀ with c₁g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂g(n) for n ≥ n₀.
g = Θ(h) gives d₁h(n) ≤ g(n) ≤ d₂h(n) for n ≥ n₁.
Chain them for n ≥ max(n₀, n₁): c₁d₁h(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂d₂h(n).
That is exactly f(n) = Θ(h(n)).
solution.trap: f = o(h) is strictly stronger than f = Θ(h) and does not follow. Θ gives a two-sided constant-factor sandwich, so it can never collapse to a little-o relation.

questions.question: Which is the correct increasing order of growth (slowest first) for large n?
options: log log n  <  log n  <  √n  <  n/log n  <  n
log n  <  log log n  <  √n  <  n  <  n/log n
log log n  <  √n  <  log n  <  n/log n  <  n
log log n  <  log n  <  n/log n  <  √n  <  n

solution.concept: Compare functions by taking ratios (or logs of both sides) as n → ∞.
steps: log log n = o(log n): log log n / log n → 0.
log n = o(√n): with n = 2^m, m / 2^(m/2) → 0.
√n = o(n/log n): (n/log n)/√n = √n / log n → ∞.
n/log n = o(n) since 1/log n → 0.
Chaining gives log log n < log n < √n < n/log n < n.
solution.trap: n/log n is easy to misplace. It sits *above* √n but *below* n; treating the /log n factor as making it slower than √n is the usual error. Verify with a concrete value: at n = 2^20, n/log₂n ≈ 52428 while √n = 1024.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: n! = O(nⁿ)
log(n!) = Θ(n log n)
2ⁿ⁺¹ = O(2ⁿ)
2²ⁿ = O(2ⁿ)

solution.concept: Exponential bases cannot be changed by a constant factor, and log(n!) is sandwiched by Stirling's bounds.
steps: n! = 1·2···n ≤ n·n···n = nⁿ, so A is true.
Stirling gives n! ≥ (n/e)ⁿ, so log(n!) = Θ(n log n); B is true.
2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·2ⁿ, a constant multiple, so C is true.
2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ and 4ⁿ/2ⁿ = 2ⁿ → ∞, so 2²ⁿ ≠ O(2ⁿ); D is false.
solution.trap: A constant added to the *exponent* is a constant factor in the value (2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·2ⁿ), but a constant multiplying the exponent is an exponential factor (2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ). Mixing these two up is the standard trap.

questions.question: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, with T(1) = 1, has the solution
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(n)
Θ(log n)

solution.concept: Master Theorem with a = 2, b = 2: compare f(n) against n^(log_b a).
steps: a = 2, b = 2, so n^(log₂2) = n¹.
f(n) = n = Θ(n¹): this is Case 2 (equal growth).
Case 2 gives T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n) = Θ(n log n).
Check by recursion tree: log₂n levels each costing n.
solution.trap: Do not report Θ(n) just because the per-level cost is n; there are log n such levels.

questions.question: Using the Master Theorem, the solution of T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n is
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n)

solution.concept: Master Theorem Case 1: f(n) is polynomially smaller than n^(log_b a).
steps: a = 9, b = 3, so n^(log₃9) = n².
f(n) = n = O(n^(2−ε)) for any 0 < ε ≤ 1.
Case 1 gives T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) = Θ(n²).
The +n work is negligible against the n² splitting cost.
solution.trap: Case 1 needs a *polynomial* gap, not just f(n) = O(n^(log_b a)). Here n is smaller by a full factor of n, so the gap is genuine.

questions.question: Using the extended form of the Master Theorem, the solution of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n is
options: Θ(n log² n)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(n log n log log n)

solution.concept: Extended Case 2: if f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^k n) with k ≥ 0, then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^(k+1) n).
steps: a = 2, b = 2, so n^(log₂2) = n.
f(n) = n log n = Θ(n¹ · log¹ n), so k = 1.
Extended Case 2 adds one extra logarithm: T(n) = Θ(n · log^(1+1) n).
Hence T(n) = Θ(n log² n).
solution.trap: Plain Case 2 would give Θ(n log n), which is *below* the actual cost — the n log n work per level already forces one extra log factor. Always check whether f(n) carries a log^k n.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² is
options: Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(n³)
Θ(n log n)

solution.concept: Master Theorem Case 2 when f(n) matches n^(log_b a) exactly.
steps: a = 4, b = 2, so n^(log₂4) = n².
f(n) = n² = Θ(n^(log_b a)): Case 2 applies.
Case 2 gives T(n) = Θ(n² log n).
Recursion tree: each of the log₂n levels costs n².
solution.trap: Reporting Θ(n²) omits the log n factor contributed by the number of levels; the per-level cost being exactly n² is the signal for Case 2, not Case 3.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n is
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n² log n)

solution.concept: Master Theorem Case 3: f(n) polynomially dominates n^(log_b a) and satisfies the regularity condition.
steps: f(n) = n log n = Ω(n^(0.7925+ε)) for ε < 0.2, so Case 3 is in play.
Regularity: a·f(n/b) = 3·(n/4)log(n/4) = (3/4)·n log(n/4) ≤ (3/4)·n log n = (3/4)f(n), and 3/4 < 1 holds.
Case 3 gives T(n) = Θ(f(n)) = Θ(n log n).
solution.trap: Option B tempts you to answer with n^(log_b a) (Case 1's answer) even though Case 3 applies here. Case 1 returns the *homogeneous* term; Case 3 returns f(n).

questions.question: For T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n, the recursion tree has total cost n at every level down to the deepest level. The solution is
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log² n)

solution.concept: Unbalanced recursion trees: add the per-level cost over the tree height.
steps: Level 0 costs n.
Level 1 costs n/3 + 2n/3 = n.
In general level k costs n as long as subproblems have not hit the base case.
The shortest root-to-leaf path has length log₃n; the longest has length log_(3/2) n.
The tree has Θ(log n) fully-charged levels, so total cost is Θ(n log n).
solution.trap: The two branch depths differ (log₃n vs log_(3/2)n), but they differ only by a constant factor 1/log₂(3/2) ≈ 1.71. Constant-factor height differences do not change the Θ-class, so the answer stays Θ(n log n).

questions.question: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 3T(n/4) + cn², the number of leaves is
options: n^(log₄3)
3n
n^(log₃4)
4^(log₃ n)

solution.concept: A tree with branching factor a and shrink factor b has a^(log_b n) leaves.
steps: Each node has a = 3 children and the argument shrinks by b = 4.
The depth is log₄n.
Number of leaves = 3^(log₄ n).
Rewrite: 3^(log₄n) = n^(log₄3) ≈ n^0.792.
solution.trap: n^(log₃4) is the reciprocal exponent (it equals 4^(log₃n)); the base of the logarithm is b = 4 and the mantissa is a = 3, never the other way round.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = T(n−1) + n, with T(1) = 1, is
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(2ⁿ)

solution.concept: A subtract-and-conquer recurrence unrolls into a sum of the per-call costs.
steps: Unrolling: T(n) = n + (n−1) + (n−2) + ··· + 1.
That is n(n+1)/2.
So T(n) = Θ(n²).
solution.trap: A single recursive call does not mean linear time. The recursion depth is n and the per-call cost is also Θ(n), so the product is quadratic.

questions.question: To prove T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n satisfies T(n) ≤ cn log₂ n by substitution, assume T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2) log₂(n/2). The inductive step requires
options: any c > 0
no condition on c

solution.concept: Substitution: substitute the hypothesis, then find the constant condition that makes the target inequality hold.
steps: = cn (log₂n − 1) + n.
= cn log₂ n − cn + n.
We need cn log₂n − cn + n ≤ cn log₂n, i.e. n ≤ cn, i.e. c ≥ 1.
So any c ≥ 1 works; the smallest integer choice is c = 1.
solution.trap: The −cn term is what makes the induction tight. Beginners assume the induction is automatically satisfied and forget that the residual n − cn must be non-positive.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = T(n/2) + 1, with T(1) = 0, is
options: Θ(log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)

solution.concept: Repeated halving with constant work per level gives a logarithmic number of levels.
steps: Unroll: T(n) = 1 + 1 + ··· + 1 for log₂n terms.
So T(n) = Θ(log n).
Substitution check: guess T(n) ≤ c log₂n; then T(n) ≤ c log₂(n/2) + 1 = c log₂n − c + 1 ≤ c log₂n provided c ≥ 1.
solution.trap: Θ(1) looks plausible because each call does constant work, but the number of calls grows with log n. The constant is per level, not per problem.

questions.question: Let f(n) = n^(log₂ n) and g(n) = n^1000. Which of the following is TRUE?
options: f(n) = O(g(n))
f(n) = Ω(g(n)) and f(n) ≠ O(g(n))
f(n) = Θ(g(n))
f(n) = o(g(n))

solution.concept: Both are n raised to a power; compare the exponents log₂n and 1000.
steps: Write both as n^(exponent): f has exponent log₂n, g has exponent 1000.
log₂n > 1000 once n > 2^1000.
Beyond that point f(n) > g(n), so f is not O(g).
f(n)/g(n) = n^(log₂n − 1000) → ∞, so f(n) = Ω(g(n)) and f(n) ≠ O(g(n)).
solution.trap: A fixed polynomial n^1000 looks enormous but any polylog exponent eventually overtakes a constant exponent. The other classic trap is assuming n^(log n) is still polynomial — it is quasi-polynomial, growing faster than every n^k.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: If f(n) = O(g(n)) then g(n) = Ω(f(n)).
If f(n) = Θ(g(n)) then 2^(f(n)) = Θ(2^(g(n))).
log(n!) = O(n log n).

solution.concept: Definitions of O, Ω, Θ, and Stirling's bound for log(n!).
steps: A: f = O(g) means f(n) ≤ c·g(n) eventually; dividing by c gives g(n) ≥ (1/c)f(n), i.e. g = Ω(f). TRUE.
B: take f(n) = n, g(n) = 2n. Then 2^(f(n)) = 2ⁿ and 2^(g(n)) = 4ⁿ, and 4ⁿ/2ⁿ = 2ⁿ → ∞, so they are not Θ of each other. FALSE.
D: log(n!) ≤ log(nⁿ) = n log n. TRUE.
solution.final: A, C and D are TRUE; B is FALSE.
solution.trap: B is the classic failure: Θ is preserved by addition and multiplication but **not** by exponentiation. Equal growth of f and g allows a multiplicative gap, which exponentiation turns into an unbounded ratio.

questions.question: Which of the following recurrences have the solution Θ(n log n)?
options: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²
T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n²

solution.concept: Apply the Master Theorem case analysis to each recurrence separately.
steps: A: n^(log₂2) = n = f(n) → Case 2 → Θ(n log n). YES.
B: n^(log₂2) = n, f(n) = n² polynomially larger, regularity 2·(n/2)² = n²/2 ≤ c·n² with c = 1/2 → Case 3 → Θ(n²). NO.
C: n^(log₄4) = n = f(n) → Case 2 → Θ(n log n). YES.
D: n^(log₂8) = n³, f(n) = n² polynomially smaller → Case 1 → Θ(n³). NO.
solution.trap: b does not have to equal 2, and a does not have to equal b; only the comparison between f(n) and n^(log_b a) matters. Option C is missed by people who assume the a = b pattern.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1, consider its recursion tree. Which statements are TRUE?
options: Every level, up to the deepest, contributes a total cost of n.
The tree has exactly n leaves.
The tree has exactly n − 1 internal nodes.
The total cost of the tree is Θ(n²).

solution.concept: Structure of a full binary recursion tree: level costs, leaf count and internal-node count.
steps: Level i has 2^i nodes, each doing n/2^i work → level cost 2^i · n/2^i = n. TRUE (for n a power of two).
Depth is log₂n, so leaves = 2^(log₂n) = n. TRUE.
A full binary tree with L leaves has L − 1 internal nodes; with L = n that is n − 1. TRUE.
Total cost = n × (log₂n + 1) = Θ(n log n), not Θ(n²). FALSE.
solution.final: A, B and C are TRUE; D is FALSE.
solution.trap: The tempting error is D, obtained by adding the leaf count n to the level cost n. Leaves do constant work at the base case, so their contribution is Θ(n), which is dominated by the Θ(n log n) internal cost.

questions.question: Which statements about the substitution method for solving recurrences are TRUE?
options: A correct guess can always be verified by induction.
If an induction attempt fails, the guess must be wrong.
Subtracting a lower-order term from the guess, e.g. guessing T(n) ≤ cn − d instead of T(n) ≤ cn, can make an otherwise failing induction succeed.
The substitution method can be used to prove tight Θ bounds.

solution.concept: Substitution is a proof technique for a *guessed* bound; the guess supplies the constant, induction certifies it.
steps: A: substitution is precisely the inductive verification of a guess, so a correct guess with suitable constants always verifies. TRUE.
B: the induction can fail purely because the guessed form is too weak, not because the bound is false — loosening the guess often fixes it. FALSE.
C: with T(n) ≤ cn − d, the residual term can absorb the extra additive work, which is exactly how T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 is proved O(n). TRUE.
D: proving both O and Ω with substitution yields Θ. TRUE.
solution.final: A, C and D are TRUE; B is FALSE.
solution.trap: A failed induction is evidence about the *guess*, not about the truth of the bound. The standard repair is to strengthen the hypothesis by subtracting a lower-order term.

questions.question: Which of the following functions are O(n log n)?
options: 5n log n + 100n
n²/log n
log(n!)
2^(log₂ n)

solution.concept: Check whether each function is bounded above by a constant multiple of n log n.
steps: 5n log n + 100n ≤ 105 n log n for n ≥ 2. YES.
(n²/log n)/(n log n) = n/(log n)² → ∞, so it is NOT O(n log n). NO.
log(n!) = Θ(n log n) by Stirling, hence O(n log n). YES.
2^(log₂n) = n ≤ n log n for n ≥ 2. YES.
solution.trap: n²/log n is larger than n log n even though the log n sits in the denominator — dividing by a log does not bring a quadratic down to n log n.

questions.question: For T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n², the solution is T(n) = Θ(n^k). Find k.

solution.concept: Master Theorem Case 1: the homogeneous term n^(log_b a) wins when f(n) is polynomially smaller.
steps: a = 8, b = 2, so n^(log₂8) = n³.
f(n) = n² = O(n^(3−ε)) with ε = 1, so Case 1 applies.
Case 1 gives T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) = Θ(n³).
Matching Θ(n^k) gives k = 3.
solution.trap: Adding the exponents of a and b (8 + 2) or answering 2 from f(n) = n² are the usual slips. The exponent is log_b a = log₂8 = 3.

questions.question: For T(n) = T(n−1) + n with T(1) = 1, the value of T(10) is ____.

solution.concept: Unrolling a subtract-and-conquer recurrence produces an arithmetic series.
steps: Unrolling to the base: T(n) = n + (n−1) + ··· + 2 + T(1).
solution.trap: Dropping the base term gives 54; the sum 10 + 9 + ··· + 1 already includes T(1) = 1, so 55 is correct.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/4) + √n, the solution is T(n) = Θ(√n · log^k n). Find k.

solution.concept: Master Theorem Case 2: f(n) matches n^(log_b a) exactly, adding one logarithmic factor.
steps: f(n) = √n = Θ(n^(1/2)), exactly matching the homogeneous term.
Case 2 gives T(n) = Θ(√n · log n).
Matching Θ(√n · log^k n) gives k = 1.
solution.trap: Because b = 4 and a = 2, log₄2 = 1/2, not 2. Getting the exponent wrong makes the comparison look like Case 1 or Case 3 and the extra log n disappears.

questions.question: To prove T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n ≤ cn log₂ n for all n ≥ 2 (with T(2) = 2) by substitution, what is the smallest integer value of c for which the inductive step goes through?

solution.concept: Substitution: substitute the hypothesis into the recurrence and require the residual to be non-positive.
steps: Assume T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2) log₂(n/2).
T(n) ≤ 2 · c(n/2)(log₂n − 1) + n = cn log₂n − cn + n.
Require cn log₂n − cn + n ≤ cn log₂n, i.e. n ≤ cn, i.e. c ≥ 1.
Base case n = 2: T(2) = 2 ≤ c·2·log₂2 = 2c, again requiring c ≥ 1.
Both conditions are satisfied from c = 1 onwards, so the smallest integer is c = 1.
solution.trap: The inductive step is *tight*: at c = 1 the residual n − cn is exactly zero. Students often answer 2 by assuming slack is needed; here the bound holds with equality at every level.

questions.question: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² with base case T(1) = 1, how many leaves does the tree have when n = 32?

solution.concept: Leaf count of a recursion tree is a^(log_b n), evaluated exactly at the given n.
steps: Branching factor a = 4, shrink factor b = 2.
n = 32 = 2⁵, so the tree depth is log₂32 = 5.
Level i has 4^i nodes; the leaves sit at level 5.
Leaves = 4⁵ = 1024.
Equivalently n^(log₂4) = 32² = 1024, which agrees.
solution.trap: Using 2⁵ = 32 (the depth) instead of 4⁵ is the standard slip — the leaf count is a^depth, not b^depth.

questions.question: Which of the following is the formal definition of f(n) = O(g(n)) for asymptotically positive functions?
options: There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ ≥ 0 such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
For every constant c > 0 there exists n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ ≥ 0 such that f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
limn→∞ f(n)/g(n) = 0.

solution.concept: Big-O is an upper bound that is allowed to be off by a fixed constant factor, and it only has to hold from some point onwards. One pair (c, n₀) that works is enough — the constant does not have to be beaten by every possible choice.
steps: Option A is exactly that statement: ∃c > 0, ∃n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) beyond n₀.
Option B quantifies c universally, so it demands f(n) ≤ c·g(n) even for c = 0.001. That is little-o, f(n) = o(g(n)), a strictly stronger claim.
Option C has the inequality reversed, which defines f(n) = Ω(g(n)).
Option D is the ratio test for little-o. It implies big-O but is not equivalent to it: f(n) = 2n is O(n) while f(n)/g(n) = 2 does not tend to 0.
solution.final: Option (A) — the existential definition of an asymptotic upper bound.
solution.trap: Reading the ∃c of big-O as ∀c, which silently upgrades the claim to little-o, or reversing the inequality and landing on Ω. The constant is a witness you are free to choose, not a quantity you must satisfy for all values.

questions.question: Let f(n) = n^(3/2) and g(n) = n (log₂ n)². Which of the following is TRUE?
options: f(n) = Θ(g(n))
f(n) = O(g(n)) but f(n) ≠ Θ(g(n))
g(n) = o(f(n))
f(n) = o(g(n))

solution.concept: Two functions are compared by the limit of their ratio. A ratio that blows up means the numerator grows faster; a ratio that tends to 0 means the denominator does.
steps: Form the ratio f(n)/g(n) = n^(3/2) / (n (log₂ n)²) = √n / (log₂ n)².
Every polynomial in n beats every power of a logarithm: for n = 2^(m) the ratio is 2^(m/2)/m² → ∞.
So f(n)/g(n) → ∞, which is precisely g(n) = o(f(n)).
Consequently f(n) = ω(g(n)) and the two functions are not within a constant factor of each other.
solution.trap: Treating (log₂ n)² as if it were a polynomial factor comparable with √n. A logarithm squared is still far smaller than any positive power of n, so option (A) and option (D) both fail; option (B) reverses the direction.

questions.question: For every integer n ≥ 2 define f(n) = n^(1 + 1/log₂ n). Then
options: f(n) = Θ(n)
f(n) = Θ(n log n)
f(n) = Θ(n²)

solution.concept: A power of n whose exponent depends on n is best read in base 2: write n = 2^(log₂ n) and push the exponent through.
steps: Split the exponent: n^(1 + 1/log₂ n) = n · n^(1/log₂ n).
Now n^(1/log₂ n) = 2^((log₂ n)·(1/log₂ n)) = 2^(1) = 2, a constant.
Hence f(n) = 2n for every n ≥ 2.
A constant multiple of n is Θ(n).
solution.trap: Assuming that an exponent containing 1/log₂ n must produce sub-linear or super-linear growth and guessing Θ(n log n) or Θ(n²). The exponent is not a fixed power: it shrinks exactly fast enough to cancel the log₂ n in the base change, leaving the constant 2.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: n^(0.1) = O(log₂ n)
log₂(n³) = Θ(log₂ n)
√n = O(n/log₂ n)

solution.concept: Each claim is settled by the limit of the ratio of the two sides. Anything with a positive power of n outgrows any power of log n, and any exponential outgrows any polynomial.
steps: (A) n^(0.1)/log₂ n → ∞ because a polynomial dominates a logarithm. So n^(0.1) is ω(log n), never O(log n). FALSE.
(B) log₂(n³) = 3 log₂ n, a constant multiple of log₂ n. TRUE.
(D) √n / (n/log₂ n) = log₂ n / √n → 0, so √n = O(n/log₂ n). TRUE.
solution.trap: Judging by a few small values: at n = 10^(6) the ratio n^(0.1)/log₂ n is still below 1, which tempts a "yes" for (A). Asymptotics is about the limit, not about the first million values — the ratio eventually climbs without bound.

questions.question: Which of the following functions grows fastest as n → ∞?
options: n^(log₂ n)
(log₂ n)^(n)
n!

solution.concept: When the bases differ and the exponents contain n, compare the base-2 logarithms of the four functions. A larger logarithm means a faster-growing function.
steps: (A) log₂ 2^(n) = n.
(B) log₂ n^(log₂ n) = (log₂ n)².
(C) log₂ (log₂ n)^(n) = n · log₂ log₂ n.
(D) Stirling: log₂(n!) = n log₂ n − O(n), i.e. Θ(n log₂ n).
Order the logarithms: (log₂ n)² is the smallest, then n, then n log₂ log₂ n, and n log₂ n is the largest.
So n! is the fastest-growing of the four.
solution.trap: Picking 2^(n) because "exponential beats everything", or n^(log₂ n) because it has a power of n in the exponent. Both are beaten by n!, whose logarithm n log₂ n exceeds n log₂ log₂ n and (log₂ n)².

questions.question: Using the Master Theorem, the solution of T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n is
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n² log n)

solution.concept: The Master Theorem compares the driving function f(n) with the watershed function n^(log_b a). Whichever is polynomially larger wins; if they match, a logarithm appears.
steps: Read a = 4, b = 2, f(n) = n.
Watershed: n^(log₂ 4) = n².
Compare: f(n) = n = O(n^(2 − ε)) for ε = 1. This is Case 1.
Case 1 gives T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) = Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Choosing Θ(n log n) because the recurrence "looks like merge sort". Merge sort has a = 2; here a = 4 quadruples the number of subproblems, so the leaves dominate and the merge cost n is negligible.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² log₂ n is
options: Θ(n³)
Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n² log² n)
Θ(n³ log n)

solution.concept: A logarithm multiplying f(n) is easily mistaken for the Case-2 signal. Decide first whether f(n) is polynomially smaller than n^(log_b a); only when it is polynomially equal does the extended case add a logarithm.
steps: Read a = 8, b = 2, so n^(log₂ 8) = n³.
Here f(n) = n² log₂ n. Since n² log n = O(n^(3 − ε)) for any 0 < ε ≤ 1, f is polynomially smaller than n³.
That is Case 1, whose solution is Θ(n^(log_b a)) = Θ(n³).
The extra log₂ n factor does not survive: the leaves number 8^(log₂ n) = n³ and each contributes Θ(1).
solution.trap: Applying the extended Case 2 because a logarithm is present. Case 2 requires f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^(k) n); here the watershed is n³ and f(n) = n² log n is smaller by a full factor of n/log n, not by a logarithm.

questions.question: In its standard form, the Master Theorem cannot be applied directly to which of the following recurrences?
options: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log₂ n
T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n²

solution.concept: The Master Theorem needs f(n) to be polynomially smaller than, polynomially equal to, or polynomially larger than n^(log_b a). A gap that is only logarithmic fits none of the three cases.
steps: (A) a = b = 2 gives n^(1) and f(n) = n is equal: Case 2, Θ(n log n).
(B) n^(1) against f(n) = n², polynomially larger and regular: Case 3, Θ(n²).
(D) n^(log₂ 4) = n² against f(n) = n², equal: Case 2, Θ(n² log n).

(C) f(n) = n/log₂ n is smaller than n but only by a factor log₂ n, which is not n^(ε) for any ε > 0. No case applies; the solution is in fact Θ(n log log n), which needs the recursion tree or the substitution method.
solution.trap: Believing that any f(n) smaller than n falls into Case 1. Case 1 demands a polynomial gap; dividing by a logarithm never produces one, so the theorem simply does not cover this recurrence.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n² is
options: Θ(n^(log₂ 7))
Θ(n²)
Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n³)

solution.concept: With a non-integral watershed exponent the answer is still read off the Master Theorem, but the exponent log₂ 7 must be left as it is — it is about 2.807, so n² is polynomially smaller than the watershed.
steps: Read a = 7, b = 2, so the watershed is n^(log₂ 7) with log₂ 7 ≈ 2.807.
Compare f(n) = n² with n^(2.807): n²/n^(2.807) = n^(−0.807) → 0, so f(n) = O(n^(log₂ 7 − ε)) with ε = 0.8.
This is Case 1, and the solution is Θ(n^(log₂ 7)).
Numerically n^(2.807) sits between n² and n³, which is why neither Θ(n²) nor Θ(n³) is right.
solution.trap: Rounding log₂ 7 up to 3 and answering Θ(n³), or matching the driving term and answering Θ(n²). A non-integral exponent is a perfectly good answer; the recurrence is not obliged to have a polynomial solution.

questions.question: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, the total cost of all the nodes at depth i (the root is at depth 0) is
options: n
n·i

solution.concept: In a recursion tree each level trades size for count: the number of nodes multiplies by a while each node's cost is divided by b. Multiplying the two gives the level cost.
steps: At depth i there are 2^(i) nodes (each call spawns two).
Each of those nodes handles a subproblem of size n/2^(i), and the non-recursive cost at that node is the same size, n/2^(i).
Level cost = 2^(i) · (n/2^(i)) = n.
Every level therefore costs exactly n; with log₂ n + 1 levels the total is n(log₂ n + 1) = Θ(n log n).
solution.trap: Multiplying only the node count, 2^(i)·n, or only the per-node size, n/2^(i). The level cost is the product of the two, and for a = b the two factors cancel exactly.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1, the value of T(16) is

solution.concept: The recursion tree of this recurrence has log₂ n + 1 levels costing n each, so the exact value is T(n) = n(log₂ n + 1) for powers of two. Unrolling the recurrence confirms it.
steps: Closed form check: T(16) = 16(log₂ 16 + 1) = 16 · 5 = 80.
The two agree, so T(16) = 80.
solution.trap: Answering 16 log₂ 16 = 64 by forgetting the leaf level, which contributes a further n = 16. The tree has log₂ n + 1 levels, not log₂ n.

questions.question: For T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1, the recursion tree for n = 8 has how many leaves?

solution.concept: Each call makes a recursive calls and the subproblem size is divided by b, so the tree has depth log_b n and a^(log_b n) leaves — the same count as n^(log_b a).
steps: Depth: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, that is log₂ 8 = 3 levels of branching.
Cross-check with the other formula: n^(log₂ 3) = 8^(1.585) ≈ 27.
(The exact sum for this tree is T(8) = 65, but the question asks only for the leaf count.)
solution.trap: Answering 8, which is the number of leaves in a 2T(n/2) tree, or 81, which is 3^(4) and comes from counting four levels instead of three. The base case is reached after log₂ 8 = 3 halvings, not 4.

questions.question: To prove T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = Ω(n log₂ n) by the substitution method, which inductive hypothesis should be assumed?
options: T(n/2) ≥ c(n/2) log₂(n/2)
T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2) log₂(n/2)

solution.concept: A lower bound is proved with the inequality pointing the same way throughout. Since the goal is T(n) ≥ c n log₂ n, the inductive hypothesis must be the same inequality applied to the smaller argument n/2.
steps: Assume T(n/2) ≥ c(n/2) log₂(n/2) — the claim at size n/2 with a ≥ sign.
Substitute: T(n) ≥ 2c(n/2) log₂(n/2) + n = c n log₂(n/2) + n.
Since log₂(n/2) = log₂ n − 1, this is c n log₂ n − c n + n.
That is at least c n log₂ n whenever n(1 − c) ≥ 0, i.e. for any c ≤ 1. The bound closes.
solution.final: Option (A) — assume the same lower bound at n/2.
solution.trap: Assuming the upper-bound form T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2) log₂(n/2). Substituting an upper bound into a recurrence can only produce another upper bound; a lower bound needs the ≥ direction, and options (C) and (D) are too weak to produce the log factor at all.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = T(n/3) + 1, with T(1) = 0, is
options: Θ(log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(√n)
Θ(log log n)

solution.concept: A recurrence that only decreases the argument without any driving function adds one unit per level, so the solution equals the number of levels, which is the logarithm of the argument in the base of the division.
steps: Unroll from n = 3^(k): T(3^(k)) = T(3^(k−1)) + 1.
After k steps the argument reaches 1 and T(1) = 0, so T(3^(k)) = k.
With k = log₃ n this reads T(n) = log₃ n = Θ(log n).
Check: T(81) = 4 = log₃ 81.
solution.trap: Answering Θ(n) because the recurrence is "linear" in its argument. The argument shrinks by a factor of 3 each time, so only the logarithm of the depth is paid; Θ(log log n) would need the argument to be square-rooted.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 with T(1) = 1, the guess T(n) ≤ c·n does not close the induction. Why?
options: Substituting gives T(n) ≤ cn + 1, which is not of the form cn; guessing T(n) ≤ cn − d closes it.
Because T(n) = O(n) is false — the true bound is Θ(n log n).
Because no constant c satisfies the base case T(1) ≤ c.
Because the Master Theorem does not apply to this recurrence.

solution.concept: The inductive step of the substitution method must land on exactly the guessed form. When the leftover additive term is positive, the guess is too weak as written and has to be strengthened by subtracting a lower-order term.
steps: Assume T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2) and substitute: T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2) + 1 = cn + 1.
The target is T(n) ≤ cn, but cn + 1 ≤ cn is false for every c.
Strengthen the guess to T(n) ≤ cn − d: then T(n) ≤ 2(c(n/2) − d) + 1 = cn − 2d + 1,
which is at most cn − d exactly when d ≥ 1. The induction now closes, and T(n) = Θ(n).
solution.final: Option (A) — the guess must be strengthened with a subtracted lower-order term.
solution.trap: Concluding that the bound is wrong (option B) or that no constant works (option C). The bound T(n) = O(n) is true; only the exact form cn is too weak to be self-sustaining. Also note the Master Theorem does apply here and gives Θ(n).

questions.question: Which of the following functions are Ω(n²)?
options: n (log₂ n)³

solution.concept: A function is Ω(n²) when it is bounded below by a constant multiple of n² from some point on. A small constant multiplier does not matter; what matters is the growth rate.
steps: (A) n²/1000 = (1/1000)·n² is a constant multiple of n²: Ω(n²). TRUE.
(B) n (log₂ n)³ / n² = (log₂ n)³/n → 0, so it grows strictly slower: NOT Ω(n²).
(C) 2^(n)/n² → ∞: TRUE.
solution.trap: Rejecting (A) because of the tiny constant 1/1000. Asymptotic bounds ignore constant factors; only the growth rate counts.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE for asymptotically positive functions?
options: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if and only if f(n) = O(g(n)) and g(n) = O(f(n)).
If f(n) = o(g(n)) then f(n) = O(g(n)) and f(n) ≠ Ω(g(n)).
For every pair of functions f and g, either f(n) = O(g(n)) or g(n) = O(f(n)).
If f(n) = O(g(n)) and g(n) = O(h(n)) then f(n) = O(h(n)).

solution.concept: The asymptotic relations are preorders on functions. Θ is the symmetric part of O, O is transitive, and O is not a total order because two functions can be incomparable.
steps: (A) Θ means bounded above and below by constant multiples, which is exactly f = O(g) together with g = O(f). TRUE.
(B) f = o(g) means f/g → 0, which gives f = O(g) at once and rules out f = Ω(g) (that would need f/g bounded below). TRUE.
(C) Fails: take f(n) = n and g(n) = n^(1 + sin n). The ratio g/f = n^(sin n) oscillates between 1/n and n, so neither f = O(g) nor g = O(f) holds. FALSE.
(D) Chaining the two constants gives f(n) ≤ c₁g(n) ≤ c₁c₂h(n) eventually. TRUE.
solution.trap: Assuming O behaves like ≤ on numbers, which would make it a total order. It is only a preorder: transitivity and reflexivity hold, but two functions with wildly oscillating ratio are incomparable.

questions.question: Which of the following recurrences have the solution Θ(n²)?
options: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n²
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²
T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n³

solution.concept: For each recurrence compute the watershed n^(log_b a) and compare it with f(n). A tie gives an extra logarithm; a strictly smaller driving term leaves the watershed exponent as the answer.
steps: (A) a = 4, b = 2 gives watershed n² and f(n) = n²: a tie, so T(n) = Θ(n² log n). NOT Θ(n²).
(B) watershed n², f(n) = n = O(n^(2 − 1)): Case 1, Θ(n²). TRUE.
(C) a = 2, b = 2 gives watershed n, f(n) = n² is polynomially larger and satisfies the regularity condition 2(n/2)² = n²/2 ≤ c n²: Case 3, Θ(n²). TRUE.
(D) a = 8, b = 2 gives watershed n³ and f(n) = n³: a tie, so Θ(n³ log n). NOT Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Assuming that a driving term equal to n² always yields Θ(n²). When f(n) ties with the watershed the answer carries an extra log n, which is exactly what makes (A) wrong.

questions.question: Consider T(n) = 3T(n/4) + c·n² for a constant c > 0. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: Every node at depth i costs c(n/4^(i))², so depth i contributes (3/4)^(i) c n².
The tree has n^(log₄ 3) leaves.
T(n) = Θ(n²), because the per-level costs form a geometric series with ratio 3/4 < 1.
T(n) = Θ(n² log n), because every level costs c·n².

solution.concept: When the number of nodes grows more slowly than the per-node cost shrinks — here 3 against 4² = 16 — the root level dominates and the geometric series converges, so the total equals the root cost up to a constant.
steps: Depth i has 3^(i) nodes, each of size n/4^(i), so the level cost is 3^(i) · c(n/4^(i))² = (3/16)^(i) c n². Multiplying the node count into the per-node cost as stated gives (3/4)^(i) c n² only if the node cost is taken as c n²/4^(i); either way the ratio is below 1. TRUE.
Leaves: 3^(log₄ n) = n^(log₄ 3), and log₄ 3 ≈ 0.79. TRUE.
The level costs decrease geometrically with ratio 3/16, so the sum is bounded by a constant times the root cost c n²: T(n) = Θ(n²). TRUE.
The level cost is not constant — it shrinks by a factor 3/16 each level — so no log n factor appears. FALSE.
solution.trap: Confusing this tree with T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, where every level costs the same and the answer carries log n. Here the branching factor 3 is much smaller than the shrink factor 16, so the root dominates.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: If f(n) = ω(g(n)) then f(n)/g(n) → ∞.

solution.concept: Compare by ratio, and remember that two exponentials with different bases are never within a constant factor of each other, while two exponentials that differ only by rewriting the same expression are identical functions.
steps: (B) 3^(n)/2^(n) = (3/2)^(n) → ∞, so 2^(n) = o(3^(n)) and the claimed direction is reversed. FALSE.
(C) 2^(3n) = (2³)^(n) = 8^(n), the very same function. TRUE.
(D) That is the definition of little-omega: for every c > 0, f(n) > c g(n) eventually, which forces the ratio to diverge. TRUE.
solution.trap: Reading O(2^(n)) as "exponential, so anything exponential is fine". A constant factor in the exponent is not a constant factor in the function: 3^(n) and 2^(n) differ by (3/2)^(n), which is unbounded.

questions.question: For T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n², the solution is T(n) = Θ(n^(k) log₂ n). Find k.

solution.concept: When the driving function ties polynomially with the watershed, the Master Theorem returns the watershed multiplied by one logarithm. The exponent k is therefore the watershed exponent itself.
steps: Read a = 9, b = 3, f(n) = n².
Watershed: n^(log₃ 9) = n².
f(n) = n² = Θ(n²), so this is Case 2 and T(n) = Θ(n² log n).
Matching against Θ(n^(k) log₂ n) gives k = 2.
solution.trap: Reporting k = 1 by counting the logarithm as part of the exponent, or k = 9 from the coefficient a. The exponent of the power is the watershed exponent log₃ 9 = 2; the logarithm sits outside the power.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1, the value of T(8) is ____.

solution.concept: Unrolling a divide-and-conquer recurrence at a power-of-two argument is exact: each level contributes n and there are log₂ n + 1 levels including the leaves.
steps: Closed form check: T(8) = 8(log₂ 8 + 1) = 8·4 = 32.
solution.trap: Answering 8 log₂ 8 = 24 by dropping the final level of leaves, which contributes another n = 8.

questions.question: For T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1, the number of leaves in the recursion tree when n = 16 is ____.

solution.concept: The leaf count of a recursion tree is a^(depth), and the depth is the number of halvings needed to reach the base case.
steps: Depth: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, that is log₂ 16 = 4 levels.
Cross-check with n^(log₂ 3) = 16^(1.585) ≈ 81.
solution.trap: Using 3 · 4 = 12 or 16 · 3 = 48 by mixing the depth with the branching factor. The leaves grow multiplicatively, so the count is 3^(4), not 3 × 4.

questions.question: Let T(1) = 0 and T(n) = T(n/2) + n for n > 1, with integer division. The smallest integer c such that T(n) ≤ c·n for every n ≥ 2 is ____.

solution.concept: This recurrence unrolls into a geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 + … whose sum is just under 2n. The constant in the bound is the supremum of T(n)/n over all n ≥ 2.
steps: Unroll: T(n) = n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 2 down to the term that reaches the base case.
The geometric sum equals 2n − 2 when n is a power of two.
So T(n)/n = 2 − 2/n, which approaches 2 from below and never reaches it.
The bound T(n) ≤ cn therefore holds for every n ≥ 2 exactly when c ≥ 2, and the smallest integer is 2.
solution.trap: Answering 1 because the first few values satisfy T(n) ≤ n. The inequality must hold for all n ≥ 2, and T(4) = 6 > 4 already breaks c = 1.

questions.question: For T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² with T(1) = 1, the exact value of T(8) is ____.

solution.concept: When f(n) ties with the watershed, every level of the tree costs the same and the total is the level cost multiplied by the number of levels. Evaluating the recurrence bottom-up gives the exact value without any asymptotics.
steps: Level-cost check: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² has watershed n^(log₂ 4) = n², so all log₂ 8 + 1 = 4 levels cost 8² = 64 each, and 4 · 64 = 256.
solution.trap: Answering 64, the root cost alone. Every one of the log₂ 8 + 1 = 4 levels costs n² = 64 here, so the total is 4 × 64 = 256 — the driving term is never negligible.

questions.question: Which statement about the standard array implementation of merge sort is TRUE?
options: It sorts in place, using Θ(1) auxiliary space.
It is stable, and it needs Θ(n) auxiliary space for the temporary merge buffer.
It is unstable, because the merge step destroys the relative order of equal keys.
Its best case is Θ(n), because an already-sorted input needs no merging.

solution.concept: Merge sort splits, sorts each half recursively, then merges two sorted runs. The merge writes into a separate buffer, so it needs Θ(n) auxiliary space, and it takes the left run first on a tie, which makes it stable.
steps: Splitting needs no extra memory, but the merge cannot be done in place without quadratic movement, so an auxiliary array of size n is allocated once.
While merging, when L[i] == R[j] the algorithm copies L[i] first. Two equal keys therefore keep their original left-to-right order, which is exactly stability.
Every input, sorted or not, goes through the same ⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 levels of merging, so no input is cheaper than Θ(n log n).
solution.trap: Mixing up "in place" with "does not move keys far". Merge sort moves keys only inside the buffer, but the buffer itself is linear in size.
solution.takeaway: Two facts travel together in every merge-sort question: stable, and Θ(n) auxiliary space for the array version.
why_wrong: (A) is false: the temporary buffer holds up to n keys at the top-level merge, so the space is Θ(n), not Θ(1).
(C) is false: stability depends on the tie rule in the merge, and taking the left key on a tie makes the algorithm stable.
(D) is false: standard merge sort does not detect sorted runs, so its best case equals its worst case.

questions.question: Quicksort uses Lomuto partitioning with the first element of the current subarray as pivot. On which input does it run in Θ(n²) time?
options: A uniformly random permutation of n distinct keys.
Keys that are already in increasing order.
Keys arranged so that every pivot is the median of its subarray.
Keys in an order in which every element is at most one position away from its sorted place.

solution.concept: Quicksort costs Θ(n log n) when the pivot splits the subarray into two parts of comparable size, and Θ(n²) when one part is empty at every level. With a first-element pivot, sorted input is the worst case.
steps: On increasing input the first element is the minimum, so Lomuto partition puts the pivot in place and leaves all remaining n − 1 keys on one side.
The next call handles n − 1 keys and again strips off the minimum, so the subproblem sizes are n, n − 1, n − 2, …
The total work is therefore (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 = Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Believing that "already sorted" is the easy case for every sort. It is the best case for insertion sort and the worst case for quicksort with an end pivot.
solution.takeaway: With a fixed end pivot, sorted or reverse-sorted input is the Θ(n²) trigger; the cure is a random or median-of-three pivot.
why_wrong: (A) A random permutation splits roughly in the middle in expectation, giving Θ(n log n) expected time.
(C) A median pivot is the best case: two halves of size about n/2, so Θ(n log n).
(D) Near-sorted input is the adversarial case, not a benign one, for a first-element pivot.
solution.faster: You do not need to sum the series: each of the n levels removes exactly one key from one side, so there are n levels of cost Θ(n) each.

questions.question: Let n = 2ᵐ. Which statement about standard merge sort on n keys is TRUE?
options: Best case Θ(n), worst case Θ(n log n).
Best case and worst case are both Θ(n log n).
Worst case Θ(n²), average case Θ(n log n).
Best case Θ(n log n), auxiliary space Θ(log n).

solution.concept: Merge sort is not adaptive: it always performs the same recursive split and the same number of merge levels, so its running time does not depend on the input order. The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) gives Θ(n log n) for every input.
steps: The recursion tree has log₂n + 1 levels because every subarray is halved regardless of its contents.
Level i holds 2ᵢ subarrays whose total length is n, and merging them costs Θ(n).
Total cost = n · (log₂n + 1) = Θ(n log n), independent of the input order.
solution.trap: Assuming that every divide-and-conquer sort has a cheap best case. Quicksort does; merge sort does not.
solution.takeaway: Merge sort: Θ(n log n) in all three cases, Θ(n) space, stable. Those four facts answer most questions on it.
why_wrong: (A) A best case of Θ(n) belongs to adaptive sorts such as insertion sort or a natural merge sort that first detects sorted runs.
(C) Merge sort never degenerates: the split is by position, not by key value.
(D) The auxiliary space is the merge buffer, Θ(n); the recursion stack is only Θ(log n).

questions.question: Quicksort is run on n distinct keys and the recursion depth is counted as the number of nested partition calls. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Best case Θ(log n), worst case Θ(n).
Best case and worst case are both Θ(log n).
Best case Θ(1), worst case Θ(n²).
Best case Θ(log n), worst case Θ(n log n).

solution.concept: Recursion depth is the height of the recursion tree, not the amount of work. A balanced split gives height Θ(log n); a maximally unbalanced split removes one key per level and gives height n − 1.
steps: Best case: each partition splits the subarray into two halves of size about n/2, so the height is log₂n.
Worst case: each partition leaves one side empty, so the sizes are n, n − 1, n − 2, …, 1 and the height is n − 1.
Height is therefore Θ(log n) at best and Θ(n) at worst; the Θ(n²) figure is the work, not the depth.
solution.trap: Reporting Θ(n²) for the depth because it is the familiar worst-case time. Depth and work are different quantities: depth n with work Θ(n²).
solution.takeaway: For any recursion question, separate the three numbers: work per level, number of levels, and the branching factor.
why_wrong: (B) ignores the degenerate split, which is reachable on sorted input.
(C) quotes the worst-case running time where the question asks for depth; the best depth is never constant.
(D) mixes the average work with the worst depth.

questions.question: Which of the following statements comparing merge sort and quicksort are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Merge sort has worst-case time Θ(n log n), while quicksort has worst-case time Θ(n²).
The array version of merge sort needs Θ(n) auxiliary space, while quicksort needs only O(log n) stack space on average.
Merge sort is stable, while the usual array quicksort is not.
Both algorithms run in Θ(n log n) time on average, and both are stable.

solution.concept: The two sorts trade different guarantees. Merge sort buys a guaranteed Θ(n log n) bound and stability with linear auxiliary space; quicksort buys in-place operation and speed in practice with a quadratic worst case and no stability.
steps: (A) True. The split of merge sort is by position, so no input can unbalance it; quicksort splits by key value and can be driven to a 0 : n − 1 split.
(B) True. The merge buffer holds up to n keys; quicksort partitions in place and keeps only the recursion stack, Θ(log n) deep on average.
(C) True. The merge copies the left key on a tie; the usual partition swaps keys across the pivot and destroys the original order of equal keys.
(D) False. The average time is Θ(n log n) for both, but quicksort is not stable.
solution.trap: Treating "Θ(n log n) on average" as a complete description of quicksort. The average says nothing about stability or about the worst case.
solution.takeaway: When two sorts are compared, hold four columns: worst case, average case, auxiliary space, stable.
why_wrong: Option (D) fails on stability alone, even though its average-time claim is correct.

questions.question: Which statement about quicksort and its pivot rules is TRUE?
options: Choosing the median of the first, middle and last elements guarantees Θ(n log n) worst-case time.
Choosing the pivot uniformly at random gives Θ(n log n) expected time on every input, while the worst case remains Θ(n²).
Choosing the pivot uniformly at random removes the Θ(n²) worst case entirely.
Quicksort becomes stable when the pivot is chosen as the smallest key of the subarray.

solution.concept: Randomisation moves the bad case from the input to the coin tosses. For any fixed input the expected number of comparisons is Θ(n log n), but there remains a non-zero probability of drawing a run of bad pivots, so the worst case is still Θ(n²).
steps: Fix an input of n distinct keys. With a random pivot, the expected split is balanced enough that the expected recursion is Θ(n log n); this holds for every input, including sorted ones.
The expectation is over pivot choices, not over inputs, so an adversary who knows the algorithm but not the coin tosses cannot force the bad case.
Some sequence of tosses still produces the degenerate split at every level, and that sequence has non-zero probability, so the worst case stays Θ(n²).
Deterministic pivot rules such as median-of-three have known adversarial inputs that force Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Confusing "expected Θ(n log n)" with "worst case Θ(n log n)". Only a selection-based pivot such as median-of-medians, or introsort's heapsort fallback, changes the worst case.
solution.takeaway: Randomisation converts a bad input into a bad coin toss; it does not delete the bad case.
why_wrong: (A) Median-of-three has adversarial inputs that keep the median-of-three at an extreme of the subarray, so no guarantee follows.
(C) Randomisation improves the expected time; it does not remove the worst case.
(D) Picking the smallest key is the worst possible pivot and says nothing about stability; stability fails because partitioning swaps distant keys.
solution.faster: A guaranteed Θ(n log n) bound needs either a worst-case linear-time pivot (median of medians) or a switch to heapsort when the depth exceeds c·log n (introsort).

questions.question: Merge sort is used to sort 8 distinct keys. Over all possible input orders, what is the maximum number of key comparisons the algorithm performs? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A merge of two runs whose lengths add to m performs at most m − 1 comparisons, and that bound is attained when the runs interleave so that one run is exhausted only at the last step. The worst case obeys M(n) = M(⌈n/2⌉) + M(⌊n/2⌋) + (n − 1).
steps: Base case: M(1) = 0 and M(2) = 1.
For n = 4 the split is 2 + 2, so M(4) = 1 + 1 + 3 = 5.
For n = 8 the split is 4 + 4, so M(8) = 5 + 5 + 7 = 17.
Each merge bound is attainable, and independent at each level, so 17 is reached by a suitable input such as alternating keys from the two halves.
solution.trap: Answering 8 log₂8 = 24, which is the number of comparisons if every level compared every pair, or 12, which is the best case n log₂n − n + 1 = 8·3 − 8 + 1.
solution.takeaway: Worst-case merge-sort comparisons: n⌈log₂n⌉ − 2⌈log₂n⌉ + 1, which gives 17 for n = 8 and 8 for n = 5.

questions.question: Counting sort is applied to n = 1000 keys, each an integer in the range 0 to 99. What is its running time?
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n + k), which here is Θ(n) because k < n
Θ(n·k)
Θ(n²)

solution.concept: Counting sort never compares keys. It counts occurrences in an array of size k + 1 and then writes the output by prefix sums, so the cost is one pass to count and one pass to place: Θ(n + k).
steps: Build the frequency array C[0..99]: one pass over the n keys, Θ(n).
Convert C to prefix sums: one pass over the k + 1 counters, Θ(k).
Write the output: one more pass over the n keys, Θ(n).
With k = 100 and n = 1000, k is dominated by n, so the total is Θ(n + k) = Θ(n).
solution.trap: Thinking that "linear time" means the key range is irrelevant. The term k is part of the cost; it is small here only because the keys are bounded by 99.
solution.takeaway: Counting sort costs Θ(n + k) time and Θ(k) space. Always quote both terms, then decide which dominates.
why_wrong: (A) Counting sort does not sort by comparison, so the n log n bound does not apply.
(C) Θ(nk) would arise from scanning the key range once per key, which counting sort does not do.
(D) Quadratic time is what the algorithm is designed to avoid.

questions.question: LSD radix sort sorts digit by digit, starting from the least significant digit. Why must each digit sort be stable?
options: Because an unstable digit sort would make the algorithm slower.
Because the order already established by the less significant digits must survive when two keys tie on the current digit.
Because radix sort compares digits with one another and needs them sorted.
Because stability is what makes radix sort in place.

solution.concept: LSD radix sort treats the digits already processed as the low-order part of the key. Two keys that tie on the digit now being sorted must keep the relative order their lower digits gave them, otherwise that earlier work is destroyed.
steps: After pass j the keys are sorted by their j least significant digits.
Pass j + 1 sorts by digit j + 1. Keys that tie on that digit must remain in the order the previous pass produced, which is exactly what a stable sort guarantees.
With a stable per-digit sort the invariant "sorted by the last j digits" holds after every pass, so after the last pass the keys are fully sorted.
solution.trap: Assuming that any correct digit sort will do. MSD radix sort can recurse on buckets, but the LSD version is correct only with a stable subroutine.
solution.takeaway: LSD radix sort = d stable passes over the digits. Stability is a correctness requirement, not an optimisation.
why_wrong: (A) Stability costs nothing asymptotically; an unstable pass would simply give a wrong result, not a slow one.
(C) Radix sort does not compare digits; it distributes them into buckets by value.
(D) Stability and in-place operation are unrelated; radix sort needs an output buffer anyway.

questions.question: Counting sort first fills a frequency array C[0..k] and then converts it into prefix sums (running totals). Immediately after that conversion, what does C[v] hold?
options: The number of keys equal to v.
The number of keys that are ≤ v, which is the last 1-based output position of value v.
The number of distinct key values that are ≤ v.
The 0-based index of the first occurrence of value v in the output.

solution.concept: The prefix-sum step turns counts into positions. After it, C[v] is the cumulative count of keys up to and including v, so a key with value v belongs at output position C[v] (1-based) once that counter is decremented.
steps: Before the conversion C[v] is the frequency of v.
The conversion sets C[v] ← C[v] + C[v − 1] for v = 1..k, so C[v] becomes the number of keys that are ≤ v.
Walking the input from right to left, each key of value v is written at position C[v] and then C[v] is decremented, which keeps equal keys in their original order.
solution.trap: Using the frequency array directly as an index, which places every duplicate at the same output slot.
solution.takeaway: Counting sort = count, prefix-sum, place right to left. The right-to-left pass is what makes it stable.
why_wrong: (A) describes the array before the prefix-sum step.
(C) counts distinct values, not keys; duplicates would then overwrite each other.
(D) the value stored is a 1-based last position, and it is decremented after each placement.

questions.question: Which statement about the Ω(n log n) lower bound for sorting is TRUE?
options: It applies to every sorting algorithm, including counting sort and radix sort.
It applies to any algorithm that learns about the input order only through pairwise comparisons; counting sort avoids it by using a key as an array index.
It states that no algorithm can sort n keys with fewer than n log₂n comparisons, and that value is exact for every n.
It follows from the fact that n! > 2ⁿ for every n ≥ 1.

solution.concept: The bound is a decision-tree argument: a comparison sort must distinguish n! possible orders, and a binary tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, so h ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n). It constrains comparison sorts only.
steps: Model the algorithm as a binary decision tree whose internal nodes are comparisons.
Each of the n! permutations must reach its own leaf, so the tree has at least n! leaves.
A binary tree with L leaves has height at least log₂L, hence h ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).
Counting sort and radix sort never branch on comparisons; they read the key as an address, so the decision-tree model does not apply to them.
solution.trap: Believing the bound covers all sorting. It covers comparison sorting; the escape route is to use the key value as an index, which requires a bounded key range.
solution.takeaway: Ω(n log n) holds for comparison sorts. Non-comparison sorts beat it by spending memory on the key range.
why_wrong: (A) is false for exactly that reason: the model presupposes comparisons.
(C) The exact bound is ⌈log₂(n!)⌉, which is about n log₂n − 1.44n, so it is strictly smaller than n log₂n.
(D) n! > 2ⁿ only from n = 4 onwards, and that inequality alone would only give h > n.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about counting sort and radix sort are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Counting sort is stable when the output pass walks the input from right to left.
Radix sort with base b over d-digit keys runs in Θ(d(n + b)).
Counting sort uses Θ(k) auxiliary space, where k is the size of the key range.
Radix sort is a comparison sort, so the Ω(n log n) bound applies to it.

solution.concept: Both algorithms trade memory for time: they use the key value as an index instead of comparing keys. Counting sort costs Θ(n + k) time and Θ(k) space; radix sort repeats a stable linear pass once per digit.
steps: (A) True. Walking right to left and decrementing the position counter places later duplicates after earlier ones, which preserves their input order.
(B) True. Each of the d passes counts into b buckets and moves n keys, so one pass is Θ(n + b) and the whole sort is Θ(d(n + b)).
(C) True. The counter array has k + 1 entries, and the output buffer adds Θ(n).
(D) False. Radix sort distributes keys into buckets by digit; it never compares two keys.
solution.trap: Assuming a linear-time sort must be comparison based. Both algorithms here are distribution sorts, and that is why they can beat Ω(n log n).
solution.takeaway: Linear-time sorts: quote time Θ(n + k) or Θ(d(n + b)), space Θ(k) or Θ(n + b), and stability of the per-digit pass.
why_wrong: Option (D) is the only false statement: it applies a comparison-model bound to a non-comparison algorithm.

questions.question: A radix sort with base b = 1000 is applied to n = 10⁶ keys, each a 9-digit decimal integer (every key is below 10⁹). Counting each pass as n + b elementary operations, what is the total number of elementary operations performed? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Radix sort needs one pass per digit in the chosen base, and one pass costs n + b operations: n to distribute the keys into buckets and b to scan the counters.
steps: The number of passes is d = ⌈log₁₀₀₀(10⁹)⌉ = 3, because 1000³ = 10⁹ covers every 9-digit decimal key.
One pass costs n + b = 10⁶ + 1000 = 1,001,000 operations.
solution.trap: Using d = 9, the number of decimal digits, instead of the number of digits in the chosen base. The base fixes d: base 1000 packs three decimal digits into one pass.
solution.takeaway: Pick the base, compute d = ⌈log_b V⌉, then multiply by (n + b). A larger base shortens d but lengthens each pass.

questions.question: Which method finds the k-th smallest of n distinct keys in Θ(n) time in the worst case, for any k?
options: Sorting the keys and reading position k.
The median-of-medians selection algorithm.
Building a max-heap and performing k extractions.
Binary searching over the key range and counting keys below each candidate value.

solution.concept: Selection is easier than sorting. The median-of-medians algorithm picks a pivot that is guaranteed to discard a constant fraction of the keys, which gives the recurrence T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + Θ(n) = Θ(n).
steps: Group the n keys into ⌊n/5⌋ blocks of five and take the median of each block by sorting five keys: Θ(n) work in total.
Recursively take the median of those block medians; that pivot has at least 3n/10 keys below it and at least 3n/10 above it.
Recurse on one side only, of size at most 7n/10.
Since 1/5 + 7/10 = 9/10 < 1, the recurrence solves to Θ(n).
solution.trap: Concluding that selection must cost Θ(n log n) because sorting does. Selection is strictly easier: it answers one question about the order, not all of them.
solution.takeaway: Θ(n) worst-case selection exists (median of medians); Θ(n) expected selection is quickselect.
why_wrong: (A) Sorting costs Θ(n log n), which is more than necessary.
(C) A heap gives Θ(n + k log n), which is Θ(n log n) when k is about n/2.
(D) Counting below each candidate is Θ(n) per probe, and the number of probes depends on the numeric range, so no Θ(n) guarantee follows.

questions.question: Randomized quickselect is used to find the median of n distinct keys. Which statement about its running time is TRUE?
options: Θ(n) expected, Θ(n²) worst case.
Θ(n log n) expected, Θ(n log n) worst case.
Θ(n) expected, Θ(n) worst case.
Θ(log n) expected, Θ(n) worst case.

solution.concept: Quickselect partitions once and recurses into the one side that contains the k-th element. The expected sum of the subproblem sizes is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n, which is Θ(n); the worst case is still the degenerate chain of partitions, Θ(n²).
steps: One partition of a subarray of size m costs Θ(m).
With a random pivot the expected size of the surviving side is at most 3m/4, so the expected total work satisfies E(n) ≤ n + E(3n/4) = Θ(n).
If every pivot is extreme, the sizes fall by one each time and the total is Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Assuming that "select instead of sort" automatically means worst-case linear. Only the median-of-medians pivot gives that guarantee.
solution.takeaway: Quickselect halves the work of quicksort by following one side; the expectation is Θ(n), the worst case Θ(n²).
why_wrong: (B) Θ(n log n) is the cost of sorting, not of selecting; only one side is explored.
(C) The worst case is quadratic, exactly as in quicksort.
(D) Θ(log n) is the recursion depth, not the work.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about selection algorithms are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Quickselect's expected Θ(n) time follows from the expected subproblem sizes forming a decreasing geometric series.
The median-of-medians algorithm attains Θ(n) in the worst case by using a pivot that is guaranteed to lie between the 30th and 70th percentile.
Sorting first and indexing costs Θ(n log n), which is asymptotically worse than the Θ(n) worst case of median-of-medians.
Any comparison-based algorithm that finds the k-th smallest of n distinct keys needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

solution.concept: Selection is a weaker problem than sorting, so it has a weaker lower bound: Ω(n), not Ω(n log n). The two ways to reach Θ(n) are randomisation (expected) and a guaranteed-fraction pivot (worst case).
steps: (A) True. With a random pivot the surviving side has expected size at most 3m/4, so the expected work is n + (3/4)n + (3/4)²n + … = 4n.
(B) True. Each block of five contributes three keys on each side of its median, so the median of medians has at least 3n/10 keys below and at least 3n/10 above it.
(C) True. Θ(n log n) dominates Θ(n).
(D) False. Median-of-medians finds the k-th smallest in Θ(n) comparisons, so the lower bound is Ω(n).
solution.trap: Quoting Ω(n log n) for selection. That bound is for producing the whole sorted order; a single order statistic costs only Ω(n).
solution.takeaway: Sort Θ(n log n), select Θ(n) expected, select Θ(n) worst case with median of medians.
why_wrong: Option (D) imports the sorting bound into a problem that does not need a total order.

questions.question: An array holds 10 distinct keys. Both the maximum and the minimum must be determined. What is the minimum number of comparisons that suffices in the worst case? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Finding the maximum alone needs n − 1 comparisons, and doing the two searches independently costs 2n − 2. Comparing pairs first makes each key lose at most once as a maximum candidate and win at most once as a minimum candidate, which brings the total down to ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2.
steps: Pair the 10 keys into 5 pairs and compare within each pair: 5 comparisons. Call the larger element the pair maximum and the smaller the pair minimum.
The overall maximum is one of the 5 pair maxima, so 4 more comparisons find it.
The overall minimum is one of the 5 pair minima, so 4 more comparisons find it.
Total = 5 + 4 + 4 = 13, which equals ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 = 15 − 2.
solution.trap: Answering 18 = 2n − 2 by running two independent scans, which wastes the information each comparison already gives about both extremes.
solution.takeaway: Paired scan for max and min: ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 comparisons, and the same pairing idea underlies the tournament method for the second largest.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about linear-time selection are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: With blocks of five, the recurrence T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) solves to Θ(n) because 1/5 + 7/10 < 1.
Grouping into blocks of three instead of five still gives a linear-time algorithm, because the fraction of keys discarded at each step stays positive.
Quickselect with a random pivot is Θ(n) in expectation even though its worst case is Θ(n²).
Every comparison-based selection algorithm needs Ω(n) comparisons in the worst case, since a key that is never examined could be the answer.

solution.concept: The block size controls how much the pivot guarantees. Blocks of five discard 3n/10 on each side, giving the 9/10 recurrence that solves to linear time. Blocks of three discard only n/3, and the recurrence then sums to Θ(n log n).
steps: (A) True. The fractions 1/5 (the recursive median-of-medians call) and 7/10 (the surviving side) add to 9/10 < 1, so the level costs form a decreasing geometric series.
(B) False. With blocks of three the pivot only guarantees n/3 on each side, so the recurrence is T(n) ≤ T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + O(n), and 1/3 + 2/3 = 1 makes the sum Θ(n log n).
(C) True. Randomisation gives a geometric expected decrease in subproblem size while leaving the adversarial worst case intact.
(D) True. An unexamined key could be the k-th smallest, so every key must be touched at least once.
solution.trap: Thinking that any constant block size works. The guarantee needs a block size of at least five, because only then is the recursive fraction sum below 1.
solution.takeaway: For median-of-medians, check the fraction sum: T(n/b) + T(cn) is linear exactly when 1/b + c < 1.
why_wrong: Option (B) is the trap: a positive discarded fraction is not enough — the two recursive fractions must sum to strictly less than 1.

questions.question: Sixteen distinct keys are stored in an array. Both the largest and the second largest key must be determined. What is the minimum number of comparisons needed in the worst case? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Finding the maximum costs n − 1 comparisons, and only the keys that lost directly to the winner can be second largest. A tournament makes each key lose at most once, so the winner has beaten exactly ⌈log₂n⌉ opponents, and the second largest is the maximum of those.
steps: Run a knockout tournament on 16 keys: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons identify the largest key.
The largest key played exactly 4 matches, one per round, so exactly 4 keys lost directly to it.
The second largest must be among those 4 losers, because every other key lost to some key that is itself smaller than the maximum.
Finding the maximum of 4 keys costs 3 comparisons. Total = 15 + 3 = 18, that is n + ⌈log₂n⌉ − 2.
solution.trap: Answering 16 + 15 = 31 by finding the maximum and then rescanning the array, which redoes comparisons that the tournament already made.
solution.takeaway: Second largest = n + ⌈log₂n⌉ − 2 comparisons; keep the list of keys each winner has beaten.

questions.question: An array of 6 distinct keys is stored in strictly decreasing order. How many inversions does it have?

solution.concept: An inversion is a pair of indices i < j with a[i] > a[j]. In a decreasing array every pair is inverted, so the count is the number of pairs, C(n,2) = n(n − 1)/2.
steps: Every one of the C(6,2) pairs of positions has the larger key first.
So the array has 15 inversions, the maximum possible for 6 distinct keys.
solution.trap: Counting ordered pairs instead of index pairs, which doubles the answer.
solution.takeaway: Sorted ascending: 0 inversions. Sorted descending: n(n − 1)/2. Insertion sort takes exactly that many exchanges.
why_wrong: (A) 6 is n, the number of keys.
(C) 21 = C(7,2) counts pairs of 7 keys.
(D) 30 = 6 × 5 counts ordered pairs twice.

questions.question: Insertion sort is run on an array of n keys that contains exactly I inversions. Which statement is TRUE?
options: It performs exactly I adjacent exchanges and runs in Θ(n + I) time.
It runs in Θ(n log n) time regardless of I.
It performs exactly I key comparisons in total.
It cannot be used to count inversions, because it destroys them as it runs.

solution.concept: Insertion sort moves a key left by swapping it with its immediate predecessor, and each swap removes exactly one inversion. The number of swaps is therefore exactly the inversion count, and the work is one pass over n keys plus one swap per inversion.
steps: Each inner-loop exchange swaps two adjacent keys that are out of order, which removes exactly one inversion and creates none.
The process stops when no inversion remains, so exactly I exchanges are performed.
The outer loop still visits all n keys, so the time is Θ(n + I).
solution.trap: Concluding that because insertion sort is Θ(n²) in the worst case, it is useless for counting. It is exactly linear in the number of inversions, which is the worst case n(n − 1)/2.
solution.takeaway: Adjacent transpositions = inversions. That identity links inversion counting to insertion sort, to bubble sort and to the Kendall tau distance.
why_wrong: (B) Insertion sort is quadratic on a decreasing array, so it is not Θ(n log n) in general.
(C) The number of comparisons is I plus the n − 1 comparisons that fail to move a key, so it is not exactly I.
(D) It can: the number of exchanges it performs is the inversion count, which is why the naive count is Θ(n + I).

questions.question: In the merge-sort based inversion count, the left and right runs are being merged and the current key of the right run is smaller than the current key of the left run. How many new inversions are counted at that moment?
options: Exactly one.
As many as the number of keys still remaining in the left run, including the current one.
As many as the number of keys still remaining in the right run.
As many as the number of keys already written to the merged output.

solution.concept: Within each run the keys are already sorted, so an inversion can only pair a left-run key with a right-run key. When the current right key r is smaller than the current left key, r is smaller than every key still in the left run, and all of them precede r in the original array.
steps: Both runs are sorted, so no inversion lies inside either run; only cross pairs matter.
Let L[i..] be the remaining left run and R[j] the current right key, with R[j] < L[i].
Since the left run is sorted, R[j] < L[i] ≤ L[i+1] ≤ …, so R[j] forms an inversion with each of them.
The count added is therefore the number of keys left in the left run, that is len(L) − i.
solution.trap: Adding one inversion per comparison. The merge step must add a whole block of inversions, which is what makes the counting Θ(n log n) rather than Θ(n²).
solution.takeaway: Merge-based counting: whenever a right key is taken, add the number of left keys still waiting.
why_wrong: (A) counts only the pair with L[i] and misses the rest of the left run.
(C) The right run keys come after R[j] in the array, so they cannot form an inversion with it.
(D) The size of the output so far has nothing to do with the pairs still unresolved.

questions.question: A permutation of n distinct keys is drawn uniformly at random. What is the expected number of inversions?
options: n²/2

solution.concept: Use linearity of expectation over pairs. For any fixed pair of positions, the two keys are equally likely to appear in either order, so the pair is inverted with probability 1/2, independently of all other pairs for the purpose of the sum.
steps: There are C(n,2) = n(n − 1)/2 pairs of positions.
For a uniformly random permutation each pair is ordered one way or the other with probability 1/2, so the indicator of that pair being an inversion has expectation 1/2.
By linearity of expectation the expected total is C(n,2) × 1/2 = n(n − 1)/4.
For n = 4 the formula gives 4·3/4 = 3, and the 24 permutations of four keys do average exactly three inversions.
solution.trap: Assuming the expectation must be a whole number. Expectations need not be integers; n(n − 1)/4 is 1.5 for n = 4.
solution.takeaway: Linearity of expectation over pairs turns an inversion-count question into a one-line computation.
why_wrong: (A) is the maximum, attained only by the decreasing order.
(C) ignores the 1/2 factor and the −1 term.
(D) is (n − 1)/2, the expected number of inversions contributed by a single key at most.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about inversions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The maximum possible number of inversions in an array of n distinct keys is n(n − 1)/2.
Two different permutations of the same n distinct keys can have the same number of inversions.
If an array has exactly one inversion, a single adjacent exchange sorts it.
The number of inversions of a permutation equals the minimum number of arbitrary element exchanges needed to sort it.

solution.concept: Inversions measure disorder in the adjacent-swap metric. Each adjacent exchange changes the count by exactly one, which is why inversions equal the adjacent-transposition distance. Exchanging arbitrary pairs is a different metric, governed by cycle structure.
steps: (A) True. There are C(n,2) pairs, and the decreasing order inverts every one of them.
(B) True. For three keys, [2,3,1] and [3,1,2] both have two inversions.
(C) True. Exactly one inversion means exactly one adjacent pair is out of order, and swapping it sorts the array.
(D) False. The minimum number of arbitrary exchanges is n − (number of cycles), for example 1 for [2,3,1], which has two inversions.
solution.trap: Treating every measure of disorder as the inversion count. Inversions count adjacent swaps only.
solution.takeaway: Inversions = adjacent-transposition distance = number of exchanges performed by insertion sort.
why_wrong: Option (D) swaps the adjacent-swap metric for the arbitrary-exchange metric; the two distances differ whenever a cycle has length three or more.

questions.question: How many inversions does the array [3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2] contain, where an inversion is a pair of indices i < j with a[i] > a[j]? Equal keys do not form an inversion. (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: With duplicates, an inversion is still a strict inequality on values but a strict inequality on positions. Equal keys never count, so the array is not simply "disordered everywhere".
steps: Count per position, looking only to the right. Position 1 (value 3): smaller keys to its right are 1, 2, 1, 2, giving 4.
Position 2 (value 1): nothing to its right is smaller, giving 0.
Position 3 (value 2): the 1 at position 5 is smaller, giving 1.
Position 4 (value 3): 1 and 2 are smaller, giving 2. Position 5 (value 1): 0. Position 6: 0.
solution.trap: Counting the equal 3s and the equal 1s as inversions, which adds 1 + 1 = 2 and gives 9. An inversion needs a strictly greater value on the left.
solution.takeaway: With duplicates, state the rule before counting: strict inequality on values, strict order on indices.

questions.question: Merge sort is applied to a singly linked list of n nodes instead of an array. Which statement about the standard top-down implementation is TRUE?
options: It cannot be used, because merge sort needs random access to the middle element.
It needs Θ(n) extra space, because a temporary array for the merge is unavoidable.
It runs in Θ(n log n) time and needs only Θ(log n) extra space for the recursion stack, because two sorted lists are merged by re-linking nodes.
It degrades to Θ(n²), because locating the middle of the list costs Θ(n) at every level.

solution.concept: Merging two sorted linked lists needs no buffer: the nodes are re-linked in place, so the only extra space is the recursion stack of the top-down split.
steps: The middle of the list is found with a slow pointer and a fast pointer in one pass, which costs Θ(n) for a list of length n.
There are Θ(log n) levels of splitting, so the middle-finding work totals Θ(n log n), not Θ(n²).
The merge walks the two lists and re-points next fields; no array and no copying is required, so the merge itself uses Θ(1) extra space.
Only the recursion stack remains: its depth is Θ(log n) for a balanced split.
Time is therefore Θ(n log n) and auxiliary space is Θ(log n).
solution.trap: Option (B) is the array intuition carried over unchanged. An array merge must copy into a temporary buffer because the elements cannot be moved out of the way without overwriting; a linked list has no such constraint, which is why merge sort is the preferred list sort and quicksort is not.

questions.question: A single call of the partition step of quicksort returns the final index of the pivot. Which conclusion follows?
options: One partition step sorts the whole subarray.
Every element left of the returned index is at most the pivot and every element right of it is greater, so later recursive calls never move the pivot again.
The partition step is stable, so equal keys keep their relative order.
Quicksort always makes exactly n recursive calls.

solution.concept: A partition rearranges the subarray so that the pivot sits between the keys that are at most it and the keys that are greater, which is exactly the pivot's place in the sorted order.
steps: Before the partition the pivot is at one end; the loop moves every key that is at most the pivot to the front and leaves the larger keys behind.
The final exchange puts the pivot between those two groups, so its index is final.
Both recursive calls then work on strict subarrays that exclude the pivot.
Hence no comparison with the pivot is ever repeated and the pivot is never moved again.
solution.trap: Option (D) confuses the number of recursive calls with the number of keys. A balanced run makes about n−1 calls, a degenerate run makes n−1 as well, but a three-way partition on equal keys can make only one. Option (C) is the classic error: the swap-based partition is not stable.

questions.question: Quicksort is run on an array of n keys that are all equal. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Both the two-way (Lomuto) partition and the three-way partition finish in Θ(n log n).
Both finish in Θ(n²).
Both finish in Θ(n).
The two-way partition takes Θ(n²), because each call removes only the pivot, while a three-way partition finishes in Θ(n).

solution.concept: A two-way partition sends every key equal to the pivot to one side, so the recursion shrinks by one element per level; a three-way partition groups the equals in the middle and stops.
steps: With all keys equal, every key satisfies key ≤ pivot, so the two-way partition returns an index at one end of the subarray.
The recursive call is then on n−1 keys, giving the recurrence T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(n) = Θ(n²).
A three-way partition (Dutch national flag) splits the subarray into keys < pivot, keys = pivot and keys > pivot.
When every key is equal, the equals group is the whole subarray, both outer parts are empty, and the recursion stops after one pass of Θ(n).
solution.trap: Assuming that a 'balanced on average' sort cannot hit its quadratic case on a friendly-looking input. Duplicate keys are a standard adversarial input for a two-way quicksort.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about quicksort are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Choosing the pivot uniformly at random makes the expected running time Θ(n log n) for every fixed input.
Recursing into the smaller part and looping on the larger part bounds the recursion depth by Θ(log n) in the worst case.
A three-way partition sorts an array with many duplicate keys in Θ(n) time.
Quicksort is a stable sort.

solution.concept: Randomisation changes the guarantee from 'for every input' to 'in expectation over the pivot choices', which is a different and often stronger statement.
steps: (A) For a fixed input the algorithm still makes random choices; linearity of expectation over the Θ(n log n) expected number of comparisons holds for each input separately. TRUE.
(B) After each partition the smaller part has at most half the keys of its parent, so the depth of the recursion is at most log₂ n whatever the pivot rule. TRUE.
(C) A three-way partition puts all keys equal to the pivot in the middle and never recurses on them, so an array of equal keys is finished in one pass. TRUE.
(D) The partition exchanges keys at a distance, which can reorder equal keys. FALSE.
